Name: Little's Law
Inputs: λ = long-run admitted throughput (req/s); W = mean residence time (s) at the same boundary; L = time-average requests present
Example Calculation: Illustrative 5000 admitted req/s × 0.05 s mean time = 250 concurrent requests on average
Rule of Thumb: Use consistent populations and finite long-run averages in stable operation; include queue time for total in-system L but exclude it for busy-server occupancy
Gotcha: Mean occupancy is not a pool maximum or percentile; typical unbounded stochastic queues require arrival rate strictly below service capacity; equality is not a general stability guarantee; rejected arrivals are excluded from the admitted population

Name: QPS from Daily Active Users
Formula: avg_QPS = DAU × actions_per_user_per_day × requests_per_action / 86400; peak_QPS = avg_QPS × peak_factor
Inputs: DAU; mean actions per active user per 24h; mean backend requests per action; measured or explicitly assumed peak factor
Example Calculation: Illustrative 10M DAU × 10 actions × 1 request / 86400 = 1157.41 QPS average; assumed 3x peak = 3472.22 QPS
Rule of Thumb: Estimate daily volume first; measure peak arrival rate at the time resolution relevant to scaling and latency
Gotcha: 3x is a scenario not a default; include retries and background traffic at the chosen service boundary; a daily mean hides bursts and QPS alone does not measure CPU cost

Name: Storage Estimation
Inputs: Retained row count; representative stored bytes per row including indexes and storage overhead; replication_factor = total full copies including primary
Example Calculation: Illustrative 1e9 rows × 200 B × 3 total copies = 600e9 B = 600 GB = 558.79 GiB before separately budgeted space
Rule of Thumb: Measure representative physical data and index sizes; budget WAL and backups and growth and rebuild free space separately
Gotcha: Do not add index overhead twice if using total relation size; no universal 30% index or compression multiplier; RF=3 means primary plus two copies; erasure coding uses a different model

Name: Bandwidth Estimation
Inputs: Per-endpoint requests/s and mean bytes/request over the same interval; compute ingress and egress separately
Example Calculation: Illustrative egress 5000 QPS × 2000 B = 10 MB/s = 80 Mbit/s; 2048 B instead gives 81.92 Mbit/s
Rule of Thumb: Use weighted mean payloads for byte accounting and measured short-window peaks for provisioning; MB=1e6 B and MiB=2^20 B
Gotcha: Request and response sizes are not generally equal; do not blindly double traffic or use a fixed protocol overhead; QPS times P95 payload is not a P95 bandwidth estimate

Name: USL (Universal Scalability Law)
Inputs: N = positive integer concurrency or node count varied in a controlled test; α and β = fitted dimensionless contention and coherency coefficients
Example Calculation: Illustrative α=0.01; β=0.001; N=10: C=10/1.18 = 8.47x single-unit throughput
Rule of Thumb: For 0 <= α < 1 and β > 0 the continuous peak is sqrt((1-α)/β); compare feasible neighboring integers and N=1
Gotcha: Fit measured steady-state throughput at several loads; coefficients and extrapolated peaks are estimates; β=0 has no finite interior peak; do not confuse normalized C with absolute QPS

Name: Amdahl's Law
Inputs: p = fraction of serial execution time parallelizable (0 to 1); N = positive integer processors
Rule of Thumb: For p<1 the asymptotic speedup is 1/(1-p); 5% serial time limits ideal speedup to 20x
Gotcha: Fixed-workload ideal bound assumes unchanged serial work and no added communication or scheduling overhead; replicas or shards do not automatically satisfy these assumptions

Name: Connection Pool Sizing
Formula: mean_busy_connections = QPS × mean_connection_seconds_per_request; candidate_pool = ceil(mean_busy_connections × (1 + headroom_fraction))
Inputs: QPS through this pool; mean sum of connection checkout durations per request in seconds; headroom_fraction >= 0
Example Calculation: Illustrative 5000 QPS × 0.005 connection-seconds/request = 25 busy connections; assumed 50% headroom gives ceil(37.5) = 38
Rule of Thumb: Use checkout-to-return time including transaction and application work while held; benchmark candidate pools against database throughput and wait-time SLOs
Gotcha: HikariCP core*2+spindles is a starting heuristic not a hard limit; no universal PostgreSQL 200-connection ceiling; sum pools across app instances; nested checkouts can deadlock regardless of average occupancy

Name: Kafka Partition Sizing
Formula: partitions >= ceil(max(target_MBps / producer_MBps_per_partition; target_MBps / consumer_MBps_per_partition; desired_active_consumers))
Inputs: Target MB/s; measured producer and consumer MB/s per partition under intended settings; desired active consumers in one conventional consumer group
Example Calculation: Illustrative target=100 MB/s; producer=5 MB/s; consumer=2 MB/s; desired consumers=30: ceil(max(20;50;30)) = 50 partitions
Rule of Thumb: Measure both producer and application consumer bottlenecks with intended replication and acknowledgments and compression; one partition is assigned to one consumer within a conventional group
Gotcha: Assumes balanced keys and adequate aggregate broker resources; hot partitions break linear scaling; 1 MB/s is not universal; the cited 2015 partition-count guidance is not a current broker limit

Name: Cache Size Estimation
Inputs: Working-set key count; representative mean allocated key-plus-value bytes including per-key metadata; separate process and buffer reserve
Example Calculation: Illustrative 100000 keys × assumed 1500 allocated B/key = 150 MB = 143.05 MiB dataset before process reserve
Rule of Thumb: Sample Redis MEMORY USAGE across actual encodings and key sizes; inspect INFO memory and leave RAM beyond maxmemory for excluded replication and AOF buffers
Gotcha: No universal 1.5-2x payload multiplier or 80/20 hit ratio; sampled key usage is not process RSS; account for fragmentation and persistence peaks without double-counting per-key overhead

Name: Disk IOPS Planning
Formula: required_IOPS = QPS × mean_device_IOs_per_query; required_Bps = required_IOPS × mean_IO_bytes
Inputs: QPS; measured device reads plus writes per query after caching and write amplification; mean IO size; volume and host IOPS and throughput limits
Example Calculation: Illustrative 5000 QPS × 4 device IO/query = 20000 IOPS; 16 KiB/IO requires 312.5 MiB/s
Rule of Thumb: Check IOPS and byte throughput and queue-depth latency together; benchmark the actual read/write mix and block size
Gotcha: Advertised IOPS are not inherently sequential; EBS SSD splits IO above 256 KiB and can merge adjacent IO; application calls are not device IO; adding disks need not bypass instance or controller limits

Name: Replication Bandwidth
Inputs: Measured replication stream bytes/s such as WAL rather than application payload; replication_factor = total copies including primary; direct primary-to-each-follower topology
Example Calculation: Illustrative 50 MB/s WAL × (3 total copies - 1) = 100 MB/s primary replication egress = 800 Mbit/s
Rule of Thumb: Provision each replication link above sustained log generation rate and reserve catch-up bandwidth; count bytes once per link rather than both sender and receiver
Gotcha: RF=1 gives zero follower traffic; cascaded topologies change primary egress; add protocol and snapshot traffic; synchronous commit waits for required acknowledgments and does not universally double latency

Name: Fanout Estimation
Inputs: Posts per period; post-weighted mean recipients selected for fanout-on-write after filtering; not the mean follower count across all users
Example Calculation: Illustrative 1M posts/day × 100 materialized recipients/post = 100M logical feed insertions/day before retries and replication
Rule of Thumb: Count one logical insertion per selected recipient; estimate hybrid push cohorts separately from read-time fetching
Gotcha: Strategy is not a numeric multiplier; prolific authors can bias fanout; no universal 10K-follower cutoff; canonical post writes and retry duplicates and physical replicas are additional work

Name: SLO Error Budget
Formula: budget_fraction = 1 - SLO; allowed_bad_events = eligible_events × budget_fraction; allowed_bad_time = period × budget_fraction
Inputs: SLO as a fraction from 0 to 1; eligible request count for event-based SLI OR period duration for time-based SLI
Example Calculation: Illustrative time-based 99.9% over 30 days: 0.001 × 43200 min = 43.2 min; request-based over 1M requests: 1000 bad requests
Rule of Thumb: For exactly 30 days: 99.99% permits 4.32 min; 99.9% permits 43.2 min; 99% permits 7.2 h under a time-based SLI
Gotcha: Request-based budgets cannot generally be converted to downtime; slow responses count only if the SLI defines them as bad; distinguish total budget from remaining budget after observed errors

Name: Memory Bandwidth
Inputs: Effective transfer rate in MT/s; useful data bits per channel excluding ECC; number of populated independent channels
Rule of Thumb: MT/s already counts transfers per cycle; multiply clock Hz by transfers/cycle only when starting from clock frequency; benchmark sustained bandwidth separately
Gotcha: DDR5-4800 is not a 4800 MHz clock; do not double DDR twice or double-count subchannels; DIMMs sharing a channel do not multiply bus width; NUMA and access-pattern penalties are workload-specific

Name: TCP Connection Capacity
Inputs: Usable ephemeral ports per source IP after reservations; reachable source IP count; distinct destination IP:port pairs; TCP source-tuple sharing enabled
Example Calculation: Illustrative Linux default with no reserved ports: (60999 - 32768 + 1) × 1 source IP × 10 destinations = 282320 possible tuples
Rule of Thumb: This is an outbound tuple-space upper bound not an inbound server connection limit; Linux default range has 28232 ports; measure file descriptors and socket memory too
Gotcha: bind-before-connect can prevent sharing across destinations; TIME_WAIT and NAT and conntrack and destination skew reduce capacity; tcp_fin_timeout controls orphan FIN_WAIT_2 not TIME_WAIT; do not disable protocol safeguards

Name: CPU Capacity from Service Demand
Formula: required_CPU = QPS × CPU_seconds_per_request / target_utilization; CPU_bound_QPS = effective_CPU × target_utilization / CPU_seconds_per_request
Inputs: QPS; measured CPU seconds per request summed across threads on target hardware; effective_CPU in CPU-seconds/second; target utilization fraction strictly between 0 and 1
Example Calculation: Illustrative 2000 QPS × 0.002 CPU-s/request / 0.5 utilization = 8 CPU units; a 2-CPU quota at 0.5 utilization gives 500 QPS
Rule of Thumb: Profile representative request mixes; include background CPU separately; a 500m CPU limit is 0.5 CPU; check quotas and cpusets and host contention before counting cores
Gotcha: CPU time is not elapsed latency; Kubernetes requests are scheduling inputs not hard ceilings and limits throttle; this is a CPU-only estimate not guaranteed throughput; serial paths and IO or memory can bottleneck first

Name: Queue Backlog Drain Time
Formula: drain_seconds = backlog_messages / (completion_rate - arrival_rate); required_completion_rate = arrival_rate + backlog_messages / target_drain_seconds
Inputs: Backlog >= 0; sustained successful completion rate and new arrival rate in messages/s; target drain duration > 0; comparable work per message
Example Calculation: Illustrative 1M queued messages / (5000 completions/s - 4000 arrivals/s) = 1000 s = 16.67 min
Rule of Thumb: Recovery capacity must process new arrivals plus backlog; estimate per partition and monitor oldest-message age; bound queues and retry budgets
Gotcha: A positive backlog has no finite drain time when completion_rate <= arrival_rate; constant-rate fluid estimate excludes warm-up and changing job costs; redelivery is extra load and processing attempts are not successful completions

Name: TCP Bandwidth Delay Product
Formula: BDP_bytes = target_bits_per_second × RTT_seconds / 8; window_bound_Bps = min(receive_window_bytes; congestion_window_bytes) / RTT_seconds
Inputs: Target per-flow data bit rate; measured round-trip time in seconds; usable receive and congestion windows in bytes
Example Calculation: Illustrative 1 Gbit/s × 0.08 s / 8 = 10 MB = 9.54 MiB in flight; a 1 MiB limiting window at 80 ms caps the estimate at 104.8576 Mbit/s
Rule of Thumb: For a sustained flow both windows need to accommodate the bandwidth-delay product; window scaling supports larger receive windows
Gotcha: Window/RTT is a bound not guaranteed goodput; loss and slow start and application or path limits reduce throughput; use round-trip not one-way delay; BDP is not a prescription for router queue size
